objective.question: Which import is correct for building an agent in LangChain v1?
options: from langgraph.prebuilt import create_react_agent
from langchain.agents import initialize_agent
from langchain_core.agents import AgentExecutor
from langchain.agents import create_agent
objective.explanation: In LangChain v1 the agent builder is create_agent in langchain.agents. The other options are older or legacy APIs that this track tells you not to use.

objective.question: You define a flight-search function with @tool but give it no docstring. During testing the model often ignores it or calls it at the wrong time. What is the most likely cause?
options: Tools without docstrings are silently dropped by create_agent
The checkpointer is missing, so tool calls are not saved
The model uses the docstring as the tool description, so it has no clear idea when to call the tool
The @tool decorator only works on async functions
objective.explanation: The docstring becomes the description the model sees when it chooses tools. A missing or vague docstring leads to wrong or missed calls. The other options misstate how @tool and the checkpointer work.

objective.question: What does create_agent return?
options: An AgentExecutor object
A LangSmith dataset
A compiled LangGraph graph that you can invoke, stream and inspect state on
A plain Python function that wraps the model
objective.explanation: create_agent returns a compiled LangGraph graph. That is why invoke, stream and state inspection all work on it.

objective.question: When does the agent loop built by create_agent normally finish?
options: When the checkpointer saves a checkpoint
When the system prompt has been sent
When the model replies with no tool calls
After exactly one tool call
objective.explanation: The loop is: model, then tools, then model again. It ends when the model gives a final answer with no tool calls. Checkpoint saves and single tool calls do not end the loop.

objective.question: Your travel agent was built with checkpointer=InMemorySaver(). A user says 'Book the flight I mentioned', but the agent has no memory of earlier turns. The invoke call passes only the messages. What is the fix?
options: Add SummarizationMiddleware
Replace InMemorySaver with InMemoryStore
Move the conversation history into the system_prompt
Pass config={"configurable": {"thread_id": "user-42"}} on every call for that conversation
objective.explanation: The checkpointer needs a thread_id at call time to save and resume state. Without it, nothing is linked across turns. Summarisation, system prompts and the long-term store do not fix a missing thread_id.

objective.question: The agent remembered conversations well in development. After the server restarted in staging, every thread starts empty. The checkpointer is InMemorySaver. What should you do?
options: Raise the SummarizationMiddleware keep value
Add HumanInTheLoopMiddleware
Switch to a persistent checkpointer such as a Postgres-backed one
Use a new thread_id after each restart
objective.explanation: InMemorySaver keeps state only in process memory, so a restart loses it. Production needs a persistent checkpointer such as Postgres. The other options do not make state survive a restart.

objective.question: Which configuration summarises older history once the conversation passes about 4,000 tokens, while keeping the latest 20 messages verbatim?
options: SummarizationMiddleware(model=..., keep=("tokens", 4000), trigger=("messages", 20))
SummarizationMiddleware(trigger=4000, keep=20)
SummarizationMiddleware(model=..., trigger=("tokens", 4000), keep=("messages", 20))
SummarizationMiddleware(model=..., max_tokens=4000, keep_last=20)
objective.explanation: trigger sets when summarisation starts and keep sets what stays unsummarised, both given as tuples. Option B swaps the two parameters, and the other options use parameter forms the API does not have.

objective.question: You want a human to review every call to a book_flight tool. The reviewer should be able to approve it, change the arguments, or refuse it. Which middleware setup fits?
options: HumanInTheLoopMiddleware(interrupt_on={"book_flight": {"allowed_decisions": ["approve", "reject"]}})
A model call limit middleware with a limit of 1
HumanInTheLoopMiddleware(interrupt_on={"book_flight": {"allowed_decisions": ["approve", "edit", "reject"]}})
PIIMiddleware("book_flight", strategy="block")
objective.explanation: approve, edit and reject cover approving, changing the arguments and refusing. Option B leaves out edit. PII and call-limit middleware do not pause for human review.

objective.question: Your agent pauses on a HumanInTheLoopMiddleware interrupt. The reviewer approves the call. How do you continue the run?
options: Call graph.get_state_history() to continue
Restart the process so the interrupt clears
Invoke the agent again with a new thread_id and the original message
Invoke the agent with Command(resume=...) carrying the decision, using the same thread_id
objective.explanation: The run is resumed with Command(resume=...) on the same thread_id, so the checkpointer can load the paused state. A new thread_id starts a fresh conversation, and reading the history does not resume anything.

objective.question: Users sometimes paste email addresses into chat. Compliance says the model must never see them. Which middleware is the best fit?
options: PIIMiddleware("email", strategy="redact", apply_to_input=True)
HumanInTheLoopMiddleware on every tool
A tool retry middleware
SummarizationMiddleware with a small keep value
objective.explanation: PIIMiddleware detects emails and redacts them in the input before the model sees them. Summarisation, human review and retries do not remove PII.

objective.question: A badly written tool keeps returning ambiguous results. The agent calls it again and again, which burns tokens. What built-in protection should you add?
options: A longer system prompt
A model call limit middleware to cap the number of model calls in a run
InMemoryStore
A second checkpointer
objective.explanation: A model call limit middleware stops runaway loops by capping model calls. Checkpointers and stores handle persistence, not loop control. Fixing the tool docstring and output still helps, but the limit is the safety net.

objective.question: You build a main travel agent with create_agent. Its tools wrap two worker subagents: a flight subagent and a weather subagent. Where should the checkpointer go?
options: On every graph, each with its own InMemorySaver
Nowhere; subagent setups cannot use memory
Only on the outermost (main) agent
On each subagent only
objective.explanation: In multi-agent setups only the outermost graph gets a checkpointer. The subagents run inside its execution. Adding checkpointers to every graph is not the recommended pattern.

subjective.question: Explain how the @tool decorator turns a Python function into a tool an agent can use. What makes a good tool definition?
subjective.answer: The @tool decorator wraps a Python function and builds a tool schema from it. The function name becomes the tool name. The type hints define the argument schema. The docstring becomes the description the model reads when it decides which tool to call. So the docstring is really a prompt. A good tool definition has a clear, specific name such as search_flights. It has typed arguments such as origin: str, destination: str and date: str. Its docstring says what the tool does, when to use it, and what each argument means, including formats like ISO dates. The tool should do one job and return compact, structured output the model can reason about. If the docstring is vague or missing, the model may skip the tool, pick the wrong one, or pass bad arguments. In real work, most 'the agent is dumb' bugs come from poorly described tools.
keyPoints: Name, type hints and docstring become the tool schema
The docstring is the description the model sees
Use clear names, typed arguments and stated formats
One job per tool, with compact structured output

subjective.question: Describe the agent loop that create_agent gives you, step by step.
subjective.answer: create_agent(model, tools, system_prompt=...) builds a compiled LangGraph graph that runs a loop. First, the model gets the system prompt and the message history. Second, the model either answers directly or emits one or more tool calls with arguments. Third, if there are tool calls, the tool node runs each tool and adds the results to the messages as tool messages. Fourth, control goes back to the model, which now sees those results and decides again. The loop ends when the model replies with no tool calls; that reply is the final answer. Middleware can hook into this loop, for example before or after model calls, or around tool calls. Because the result is a compiled graph, you can invoke it, stream it, add a checkpointer, and inspect state. To guard against endless cycles, add a model call limit middleware.
keyPoints: Model receives the system prompt and the messages
Tool calls run and their results are added as tool messages
The loop repeats until the model replies with no tool calls
It is a compiled LangGraph graph, so invoke, stream and state all work
Middleware hooks in; a call limit stops runaway loops

subjective.question: Walk through how you would build the week's travel agent with flight-search and weather tools.
subjective.answer: First I define two tools with @tool: search_flights(origin, destination, date) and get_weather(city, date). Each has a docstring that explains its purpose and argument formats. In development they can return mocked data. Next I write a system prompt. It tells the agent to confirm the destination and dates, search flights, check the weather at the destination for the travel date, and then give a short recommendation. Then I call create_agent(model, tools=[search_flights, get_weather], system_prompt=..., checkpointer=InMemorySaver()), imported from langchain.agents. I invoke it with {"messages": [...]} and config={"configurable": {"thread_id": "trip-1"}}. To meet the checkpoint, I send a multi-turn conversation on one thread and check that the tools are called in a sensible order. I also check that a follow-up like 'what about the day after?' reuses earlier context. I enable LangSmith tracing to see each tool call in the trace.
keyPoints: Two well-documented @tool functions
A system prompt that guides the order of tool calls
create_agent with tools, system_prompt and checkpointer
Use a thread_id per conversation and test follow-ups
Verify the tool order using LangSmith traces

subjective.question: Why does short-term memory need both a checkpointer and a thread_id? What happens if either is missing?
subjective.answer: The checkpointer is the storage layer. You pass it to create_agent at build time. After each step of the graph, it saves a snapshot of the agent's state, mainly the message list. The thread_id is the key that says which conversation a call belongs to. You pass it at call time in config={"configurable": {"thread_id": "..."}}. If there is no checkpointer, nothing is saved, so every call starts from scratch. If there is a checkpointer but no thread_id, it cannot save or resume, because it does not know which thread to write to or read from. With both in place, each call on the same thread_id loads the previous state, adds the new message and continues. Different thread_ids give separate conversations. That is how one deployed agent serves many users without mixing their histories.
keyPoints: Checkpointer at build time, thread_id at call time
The checkpointer saves state snapshots per thread
No checkpointer means no memory
No thread_id means it cannot save or resume
Separate thread_ids isolate users

subjective.question: Compare InMemorySaver with a persistent checkpointer. When would you use each, and what changes on the Agent Server?
subjective.answer: InMemorySaver keeps checkpoints in the Python process memory. It needs no setup, so it suits notebooks, unit tests and local development. But all state is lost when the process restarts. It also cannot be shared across several server instances. A persistent checkpointer, for example one backed by Postgres, writes checkpoints to a database. Conversations then survive restarts and deployments, and all replicas can share them. That is what production needs, along with care about database sizing and retention. When you deploy on the Agent Server, persistence is handled automatically, so you do not wire up your own checkpointer there. In code, the agent logic stays the same in all cases. Only the checkpointer you pass, or the platform, changes. That keeps moving from prototype to production simple.
keyPoints: InMemorySaver is process-local and lost on restart
Good for dev and tests only
Use a persistent checkpointer such as Postgres in production
Agent Server handles persistence automatically
Agent code does not change, only the persistence layer

subjective.question: What is middleware in LangChain v1 agents, and why is it the main customisation primitive?
subjective.answer: Middleware is code that hooks into the agent loop. You pass it as create_agent(..., middleware=[...]), and the classes live in langchain.agents.middleware. Middleware can run before or after the model call, wrap model or tool calls, and change state, messages or requests. Instead of rewriting the agent graph, you stack small, reusable behaviours. Built-ins cover common needs: SummarizationMiddleware for long histories, HumanInTheLoopMiddleware for approvals, PIIMiddleware for guardrails, plus model fallback, tool retry, model call limits and LLM-based tool selection. You can also write custom middleware, for example to log, inject context or enforce business rules. This design keeps the core loop standard and well-tested, while letting you shape behaviour in a clear and testable way. The order of middleware in the list matters, so think about which should run first.
keyPoints: Hooks into the agent loop around model and tool calls
Passed as a list to create_agent
Built-ins: summarisation, HITL, PII, fallback, retry, call limits, tool selection
Custom middleware handles your own rules
Avoids rewriting the graph; order matters

subjective.question: Explain SummarizationMiddleware. How would you choose its trigger and keep values?
subjective.answer: Long conversations grow the message list. That raises cost and latency, and it can eventually overflow the context window. SummarizationMiddleware fixes this. When a threshold is reached, it uses a model to summarise older messages and keeps only the recent ones verbatim. You configure it as SummarizationMiddleware(model=..., trigger=("tokens", 4000), keep=("messages", 20)). trigger says when to summarise, here once history passes about 4,000 tokens. keep says how much recent history stays untouched, here the last 20 messages. To choose values, I look at the model's context window and my cost budget. The trigger sits well below the limit, leaving room for the system prompt, tool schemas and tool outputs. keep should be large enough to hold the active task, such as the current flight options. Often a cheaper model can do the summarising. I check in LangSmith traces that key facts like dates and destinations survive the summary.
keyPoints: Prevents context overflow, cost growth and latency
trigger sets when; keep sets what stays verbatim
Leave headroom for prompts, schemas and tool outputs
A cheaper model can summarise
Check in traces that key facts survive

subjective.question: How does HumanInTheLoopMiddleware work end to end, including pausing and resuming?
subjective.answer: You configure it with interrupt_on, which maps tool names to policies. For example: HumanInTheLoopMiddleware(interrupt_on={"book_flight": {"allowed_decisions": ["approve", "edit", "reject"]}}). When the model proposes a call to book_flight, the middleware raises an interrupt before the tool runs. The graph pauses, and the checkpointer saves the state. So a checkpointer and a thread_id are required. Your app shows the pending call to a reviewer. The reviewer approves it, edits the arguments, or rejects it. You then resume by invoking the agent with Command(resume=...) carrying that decision, on the same thread_id. On approve, the tool runs as proposed. On edit, it runs with the changed arguments. On reject, the tool does not run and the model is told it was refused. Tools that are safe, like get_weather, are simply left out of interrupt_on.
keyPoints: interrupt_on maps tools to allowed_decisions
Decisions are approve, edit and reject
The pause relies on a checkpointer and thread_id
Resume with Command(resume=...) on the same thread_id
Only gate risky tools

subjective.question: What guardrails would you add to a production travel agent, and how does PIIMiddleware fit in?
subjective.answer: Guardrails limit what goes into and out of the agent and what it is allowed to do. For data protection, I use PIIMiddleware, for example PIIMiddleware("email", strategy="redact", apply_to_input=True). It detects email addresses in user input and redacts them before the model sees them. I can add more instances for other PII types the business cares about. For risky actions such as booking or payments, I add HumanInTheLoopMiddleware approval. For cost and stability, I add a model call limit to stop runaway loops. Tool retry middleware handles flaky APIs, and model fallback covers provider outages. I also scope the tools themselves: a read-only search tool cannot book anything. If needed, I add custom middleware for business rules, such as blocking bookings outside allowed dates. Finally, I monitor everything in LangSmith traces.
keyPoints: PIIMiddleware redacts emails before the model sees them
HITL approval for risky actions
Call limits, tool retry and model fallback for stability
Least-privilege tool design
Custom middleware for business rules, plus tracing

subjective.question: Your travel agent sometimes checks the weather before it knows the destination, or skips the flight search. How do you debug and fix the tool-calling order?
subjective.answer: First, I reproduce the problem with LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and inspect the trace. It shows each model call, the tool calls chosen, their arguments and their results. Usually the cause is one of three things. The first is vague tool docstrings. I make them explicit, for example 'Use after the destination and date are known'. I also make argument formats clear. The second is a weak system prompt. I spell out the workflow: confirm the destination and dates, search flights, then check the weather for the destination on the travel date, then summarise. The third is poor tool outputs. If search_flights returns messy text, the model may misread it, so I return compact structured data. I keep tools focused, so the model is not choosing among many overlapping ones. Then I rerun a fixed set of test conversations and compare traces, ideally as a small LangSmith dataset, to confirm the order is now stable.
keyPoints: Use LangSmith traces to see the call order and arguments
Sharpen tool docstrings, including when to use each tool
State the workflow in the system prompt
Return structured, compact tool outputs
Retest with fixed conversations

subjective.question: Because create_agent returns a compiled LangGraph graph, what practical capabilities do you get? Give examples.
subjective.answer: Since the agent is a compiled LangGraph graph, all the graph features apply. I can call invoke for a single result. I can stream to show tokens and tool steps live in a UI; stream_events with version="v3" is the recommended way to drive a graph, and it surfaces interrupts. With a checkpointer and a thread_id, I get per-thread memory. I can inspect the current state for a thread. graph.get_state_history(config) lists checkpoints newest first, which is very useful for debugging what the agent saw at each step. Interrupts from HumanInTheLoopMiddleware are resumed with Command(resume=...). The agent can also be used as a node or wrapped as a tool inside a larger system, such as the subagents pattern. Finally, it runs locally with langgraph dev and can be viewed in LangSmith Studio, or deployed on the Agent Server, which handles persistence for me.
keyPoints: invoke and streaming, with stream_events v3 recommended
State inspection and get_state_history, newest first
Interrupts resumed with Command(resume=...)
Composable into the subagents pattern
Works with langgraph dev, Studio and the Agent Server

subjective.question: When would you move from a single create_agent to a subagents design or a Deep Agent, and how is memory handled there?
subjective.answer: A single create_agent is enough while the tool set is small and the task is short. I move to the subagents pattern when the domains split clearly, for example flights, hotels and visas. In that pattern, a main create_agent has tools that each wrap a worker subagent with its own prompt and tools. This keeps each context focused and makes the tool choice easier. The older langgraph-supervisor package is no longer actively maintained, so I use this pattern instead. For long-running, multi-step tasks such as planning a full itinerary with research and notes, create_deep_agent is useful. It pre-assembles filesystem tools, summarisation, subagents and prompt caching. For memory, only the outermost graph gets a checkpointer, and the thread_id is passed at the top level. The subagents run within that execution. On the Agent Server, persistence is handled automatically.
keyPoints: Single agent for small tool sets and short tasks
Subagents pattern: main agent tools wrap worker agents
langgraph-supervisor is not actively maintained
create_deep_agent for long-running tasks
Checkpointer only on the outermost graph

steps.overview: This step teaches retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) the LangChain v1 way. You load and split PDFs, embed the chunks into a vector store, and expose retrieval as a tool that a create_agent agent calls when it needs evidence. RAG with honest citations is a core LangChain Academy topic and a very common interview task, because it shows you can ground an LLM in private data and prevent hallucination.
objectives: Load a folder of PDFs into LangChain Documents and split them into chunks while keeping page metadata.
Embed chunks and index them in a vector store, then query it with similarity search.
Wrap a retriever as a tool and give it to an agent built with create_agent.
Write a system prompt and tool output format that make the agent cite file and page, and say 'I don't know' when evidence is missing.
Trace and debug retrieval quality in LangSmith by inspecting the tool call inputs and returned chunks.

concepts.explanation: A LangChain Document has page_content (text) and metadata (a dict). PyPDFLoader produces one Document per PDF page, with metadata such as 'source' (file path) and 'page'. Citations depend entirely on this metadata surviving every later step.

Loaders turn files or URLs into Documents. PyPDFLoader loads one PDF, and PyPDFDirectoryLoader loads every PDF in a folder. Both live in langchain_community.document_loaders and need the pypdf package installed.

Splitters cut long Documents into smaller chunks that fit the embedding model and give precise retrieval. RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter from langchain_text_splitters is the recommended default. It splits on paragraphs, then lines, then words. split_documents copies each parent's metadata into every chunk, so page numbers are kept.

chunk_size is the maximum characters per chunk. chunk_overlap repeats some characters between neighbouring chunks so a sentence is not lost at a boundary. The official tutorials use 1000 and 200 as a starting point. Tune both against your own questions, not by guesswork.

An embedding model maps text to a vector, so similar meanings land close together. Examples are OpenAIEmbeddings (langchain_openai) and HuggingFaceEmbeddings (langchain_huggingface). You must embed the query with the same model you used to index the documents.

A vector store saves chunk vectors and returns the nearest ones for a query, for example with similarity_search(query, k=4). InMemoryVectorStore (langchain_core.vectorstores) is good for learning. Chroma, FAISS, PGVector (Postgres) or a managed store suit persistence and scale. as_retriever() turns any store into a Runnable retriever.

In agentic RAG, retrieval is a tool the model decides to call, and it can rewrite the query or search again. You define it with the @tool decorator, using a clear docstring because the model reads it to decide when to call. With response_format='content_and_artifact', the tool returns text for the model plus the raw Documents as an artifact for your code.

The tool output labels each chunk, for example [manual.pdf p.12], so the model can copy exact references. The system prompt tells the agent to answer only from retrieved text, cite every claim, and reply 'I don't know' if the passages do not contain the answer. This is what the checkpoint tests.

keyFacts: Build the agent with create_agent(model, tools=[...], system_prompt=...) from langchain.agents. It returns a compiled LangGraph graph, so you call invoke or stream on it.
PyPDFLoader 'page' metadata is 0-indexed. Add 1 before showing it to users, or use 'page_label' where it is present, so citations match the printed page.
RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=1000, chunk_overlap=200, add_start_index=True) is the official tutorial default. add_start_index records each chunk's character offset in metadata.
Index and query must use the same embedding model. If you change the model, re-embed the whole corpus.
similarity_search(query, k=4) returns the top-k chunks. A higher k improves recall but costs more tokens and adds noise.
@tool(response_format='content_and_artifact') must return a tuple (content, artifact). The artifact is not sent to the model.
InMemoryVectorStore is lost when the process restarts. Use a persistent store for anything you will ship.
Agentic RAG (retrieval as a tool) lets the model skip retrieval for small talk and search several times. A 2-step chain always retrieves exactly once and is cheaper and more predictable.

With LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY set, each tool call and its retrieved chunks appear in the trace. Use the trace to check whether a wrong answer was a retrieval miss or a generation error.

example.caption: Q&A agent over a PDF folder that cites file and page, and admits when it does not know
example.code:
from pathlib import Path
from langchain_community.document_loaders import PyPDFDirectoryLoader
from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter
from langchain_huggingface import HuggingFaceEmbeddings
from langchain_core.vectorstores import InMemoryVectorStore
from langchain.tools import tool
from langchain.agents import create_agent

docs = PyPDFDirectoryLoader("pdfs/").load()  # one Document per page
splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=1000, chunk_overlap=200, add_start_index=True)
chunks = splitter.split_documents(docs)  # metadata (source, page) is copied to chunks
store = InMemoryVectorStore(HuggingFaceEmbeddings(model_name="sentence-transformers/all-mpnet-base-v2"))
store.add_documents(chunks)

@tool(response_format="content_and_artifact")
def search_docs(query: str):
    """Search the company PDF library. Returns passages labelled with file name and page."""
    hits = store.similarity_search(query, k=4)
    text = "\n\n".join(f"[{Path(d.metadata['source']).name} p.{d.metadata['page'] + 1}]\n{d.page_content}" for d in hits)
    return text, hits

PROMPT = ("Answer ONLY from passages returned by search_docs. Cite every claim like [file.pdf p.N], "
          "copying labels exactly. If the passages do not contain the answer, reply exactly: I don't know.")
agent = create_agent("anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5", tools=[search_docs], system_prompt=PROMPT)

for q in ["What is the refund window?", "Who won the 2011 Cricket World Cup?"]:
    out = agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": q}]})
    print(q, "->", out["messages"][-1].content)

pitfalls: Showing 0-indexed page numbers. This gives citations that are off by one, and the checkpoint fails even though retrieval worked.
Losing metadata. This happens if you build new Documents from plain strings or join chunks without labels, because the model then has nothing real to cite and will invent page numbers.
A vague tool docstring such as 'search tool'. The model may skip the tool and answer from its own memory, which breaks both grounding and the 'I don't know' rule.
Testing only questions the documents answer. Always include out-of-scope questions, because without a strict refusal instruction the model answers them from general knowledge.
Mixing embedding models, or forgetting to re-index after changing chunk settings. Similarity scores then become meaningless and recall drops silently.
Setting k too high or chunks too large. This floods the context with irrelevant text, raises cost and can push the model to cite the wrong page.
