objective.question: You load a PDF with PyPDFLoader. A chunk's metadata shows page=11 and has no page_label key. Which page number should your agent show the user so the citation matches the printed page?
options: Page 12
The chunk's start_index value
Page 10
Page 11
objective.explanation: PyPDFLoader's 'page' metadata is 0-indexed, so you add 1 before showing it to users. Showing 11 is off by one, 10 subtracts in the wrong direction, and start_index is a character offset, not a page.

objective.question: In a LangChain Document, where should the source file name and page number be stored so they survive splitting and can be cited later?
options: In the vector store's index name
In the Document's metadata dictionary
In the agent's system prompt
Appended to page_content as plain text
objective.explanation: A Document has page_content and metadata. Text splitters copy metadata to every chunk, so source and page stay attached. Putting them in page_content pollutes the embeddings, and the index name or system prompt cannot identify individual chunks.

objective.question: What is the main purpose of chunk_overlap=200 in RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=1000, chunk_overlap=200)?
options: To limit each chunk to 200 tokens
To remove duplicate chunks before embedding
To reserve 200 characters for metadata
To keep sentences or ideas that cross a chunk boundary present in both neighbouring chunks
objective.explanation: Overlap repeats the end of one chunk at the start of the next, so context that falls on a boundary is not lost. It does not set a token limit, deduplicate chunks or store metadata.

objective.question: You set add_start_index=True on your text splitter. What does this add to each chunk?
options: The page number from the original PDF
A unique UUID used as the vector store ID
The character offset where the chunk starts in the parent document
A sequential chunk number starting at 0
objective.explanation: add_start_index records each chunk's character offset within the original Document in metadata as start_index. It is not a chunk counter, a page number or a vector store ID.

objective.question: Your team indexed 5,000 PDF pages with embedding model A. A developer switches the query side to a newer embedding model B for better quality. Retrieval results become nonsense. What is the correct fix?
options: Re-embed the whole corpus with model B, or revert queries to model A
Normalise the query vectors to unit length
Lower chunk_size so vectors match better
Increase k from 4 to 20 to compensate
objective.explanation: The index and the query must use the same embedding model, because vectors from different models live in different spaces. A larger k, smaller chunks or normalisation cannot make incompatible vectors comparable.

objective.question: Your Q&A agent sometimes misses the relevant passage. A colleague suggests raising similarity_search k from 4 to 15. What is the most accurate trade-off?
options: Precision improves and cost falls
There is no trade-off; higher k is always better
It changes nothing, because k only affects the reranker
Recall usually improves, but token cost and noise in the context also rise
objective.explanation: A higher k returns more chunks, so the right one is more likely included. The model then reads more tokens and more irrelevant text, which can lower answer quality. similarity_search has no reranker that k controls.

objective.question: You define a retrieval tool with @tool(response_format='content_and_artifact'). What must the function return, and what does the model see?
options: A dict with 'content' and 'artifact' keys; the model sees both
A tuple (content, artifact); the model sees only the content, and the artifact is kept on the ToolMessage for your code
A list of Documents; the model sees the raw Document objects
A single string; the model sees the string and the metadata
objective.explanation: With response_format='content_and_artifact' the tool must return a tuple (content, artifact). Only the content is sent to the model. The artifact, for example the raw Documents, stays on the ToolMessage for downstream use such as building citations.

objective.question: Your demo Q&A agent uses InMemoryVectorStore. After a server restart, every question gets 'I don't know'. Why?
options: InMemoryVectorStore data is lost when the process restarts, so the index is empty
create_agent clears tools on restart
The checkpointer deleted the vectors
The embedding model's API key expired
objective.explanation: InMemoryVectorStore holds vectors only in process memory, so a restart wipes them. For anything you ship, use a persistent vector store. The checkpointer stores graph state, not vectors, and create_agent does not clear tools.

objective.question: A compliance team needs a document Q&A service with predictable latency and cost: every request must retrieve exactly once, and users never make small talk. Which design fits best?
options: A deep agent created with create_deep_agent
A 2-step chain that always retrieves once, then generates
A multi-agent subagents pattern
Agentic RAG with the retriever exposed as a tool
objective.explanation: A 2-step chain retrieves exactly once per request, so it is cheaper and more predictable. Agentic RAG lets the model skip retrieval or search several times, which is flexible but less predictable. Deep agents and subagents add overhead that this task does not need.

objective.question: You built agent = create_agent(model, tools=[retrieve_context], system_prompt=...). How do you ask it a question?
options: agent.run("What is the refund period?")
retrieve_context.invoke("What is the refund period?") and return the result directly
agent.compile().invoke("What is the refund period?")
agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is the refund period?"}]})
objective.explanation: create_agent returns a compiled LangGraph graph, so you call invoke or stream with a state containing messages. It is already compiled, so there is no .run. Calling the tool directly skips the model and the agent loop.

objective.question: A user reports a wrong answer. In the LangSmith trace, the retrieval tool call returned four chunks, and none of them contains the needed fact. The fact does exist on page 37 of a loaded PDF. What kind of failure is this?
options: A checkpointer failure
A tracing bug, because LangSmith hides some chunks
A retrieval miss: the right chunk was never retrieved
A generation error: the model ignored the context
objective.explanation: If the retrieved chunks do not contain the answer, the model never had the right evidence, so this is a retrieval miss. You would fix chunking, k, the query or the embeddings. A generation error would show the correct chunk in the trace but a wrong answer.

objective.question: Your checkpoint requires an honest 'I don't know' for questions outside the PDFs. Testing shows the agent answers 'Who won the 2011 Cricket World Cup?' from general knowledge. What is the most effective first change?
options: Tighten the system prompt: answer only from retrieved context, cite pages, and say 'I don't know' when the context does not contain the answer
Increase chunk_overlap to 500
Switch to a larger embedding model
Remove the retrieval tool so the model cannot be confused
objective.explanation: The behaviour comes from the model using its own knowledge, so the fix is a grounding instruction that limits answers to retrieved context and defines the refusal. Removing the tool breaks the agent. Overlap and embedding changes affect retrieval, not whether the model refuses.

subjective.question: What is a LangChain Document, and why does metadata matter so much in a RAG system that must cite sources?
subjective.answer: A Document is the basic unit of text in LangChain. It has page_content, which is the text, and metadata, which is a dictionary of facts about that text. Loaders fill metadata for you. PyPDFLoader, for example, adds the source path and page number. Metadata matters because it is the only reliable link between a retrieved chunk and its origin. When I split documents, the splitter copies metadata to every chunk, so even a small chunk still knows its file and page. At answer time I read the metadata from the retrieved chunks to build citations. I keep metadata out of page_content, because putting it in the text pollutes the embedding. I can also add my own fields, such as department or version, and use them for filtering.
keyPoints: Document = page_content + metadata
Loaders populate source and page metadata
Splitters copy metadata to every chunk
Citations are built from metadata, not guessed by the model
Keep metadata out of the embedded text

subjective.question: Walk through the indexing pipeline for a folder of PDFs, from files on disk to a searchable vector store.
subjective.answer: First I load. For each PDF I use PyPDFLoader, or a directory loader, which returns one Document per page with source and page metadata. Second I split. I use RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter with chunk_size=1000, chunk_overlap=200 and add_start_index=True, the official tutorial default. It tries paragraph, then line, then word boundaries, so chunks stay readable, and each chunk keeps its page metadata plus a start_index offset. Third I embed. I pick one embedding model and use it for both indexing and queries. Fourth I store. I call add_documents on a vector store. For a demo InMemoryVectorStore is fine, but it is lost on restart, so for anything shipped I use a persistent store. Finally I test with similarity_search(query, k=4) and check that the right pages come back before I wire it into the agent.
keyPoints: Load: one Document per page with metadata
Split with RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter and keep metadata
Embed with one consistent model
Store in a vector store, persistent for production
Sanity-check retrieval before building the agent

subjective.question: How do you choose chunk_size and chunk_overlap? What goes wrong if chunks are too small or too large?
subjective.answer: I start with the tutorial default of 1000 characters and 200 overlap, then tune against real questions. If chunks are too small, each one lacks context. A definition may be cut from its condition, the embedding becomes vague, and I need a higher k to collect enough evidence. If chunks are too large, one vector has to represent several topics, so similarity becomes blurry. Each retrieved chunk also costs more tokens and adds noise. Overlap protects ideas that fall across a boundary. Too little overlap loses them. Too much overlap wastes storage and returns near-duplicate chunks. The document type matters too. Dense legal clauses need different settings from short FAQ entries. I measure the effect with a small LangSmith dataset rather than guessing.
keyPoints: Start from 1000/200 and tune with real queries
Too small: lost context, vague embeddings, needs higher k
Too large: blurred similarity, more tokens, more noise
Overlap guards boundary context but adds duplication
Validate with an evaluation dataset

subjective.question: Why must the index and the query use the same embedding model? What is your plan if the business wants to upgrade the model?
subjective.answer: An embedding model maps text to a vector space that is specific to that model. Distances only mean something inside one space. If I index with model A and query with model B, the vectors are not comparable. Retrieval returns near-random chunks, and nothing raises an error, so the failure is silent. That makes it dangerous. To upgrade, I treat it as a migration. I build a new index by re-embedding the whole corpus with the new model, ideally into a separate collection. I run my LangSmith evaluation dataset against both indexes and compare retrieval quality and answer correctness. If the new one is better, I switch the query side and the index together, then retire the old index. I also record the embedding model name with the index so a mismatch is easy to spot.
keyPoints: Vectors are only comparable within one model's space
A mismatch fails silently with poor retrieval
Upgrade means re-embedding the whole corpus
Build a parallel index and compare with evaluations
Switch index and query model together

subjective.question: Explain how you expose a retriever as a tool for an agent built with create_agent, including why you might use response_format='content_and_artifact'.
subjective.answer: I write a Python function decorated with @tool, with a clear docstring such as 'Search the company PDFs for information'. The model reads the docstring to decide when to call it. Inside, the function runs vector_store.similarity_search(query, k=4). With response_format='content_and_artifact' the function must return a tuple. The first item is content: a string that joins each chunk's text with its source and page, which the model reads. The second item is the artifact: the raw Document list, which is not sent to the model but is kept on the ToolMessage. My application code can then build accurate citation links from the real metadata. I then call create_agent(model, tools=[retrieve_context], system_prompt=...). It returns a compiled LangGraph graph, which I call with invoke or stream.
keyPoints: @tool with a descriptive docstring guides tool choice
Run similarity_search inside the tool
content_and_artifact requires a (content, artifact) tuple
Artifact is not sent to the model; it is used for citations in code
create_agent returns a compiled graph; use invoke or stream

subjective.question: Design the citation behaviour for the PDF Q&A agent so that cited pages are always real and match the printed page.
subjective.answer: Citations must come from metadata, not from the model's memory. In the retrieval tool I format each chunk as a block with its source file and page, so the model can only cite pages it actually saw. PyPDFLoader's page field is 0-indexed, so I add 1 before displaying it, or use page_label where it is present, because that matches printed numbering such as roman-numeral front matter. The system prompt tells the model to cite the file and page for every claim, using only the pages shown in the context. As a safety check, my code compares the cited pages in the answer against the artifact Documents from the tool call and flags any page that was not retrieved. In LangSmith I spot-check traces to confirm the cited page contains the quoted fact.
keyPoints: Citations come from chunk metadata shown in context
PyPDFLoader page is 0-indexed: add 1 or use page_label
Prompt requires a citation for each claim from given pages only
Validate cited pages against the tool artifact
Spot-check traces in LangSmith

subjective.question: How do you make the agent say 'I don't know' for questions the documents cannot answer, without making it refuse valid questions?
subjective.answer: I combine prompt rules with testing. The system prompt says: answer only from the retrieved context; if the context does not contain the answer, say 'I don't know, this is not covered in the documents'; never use outside knowledge. Then I test both sides. I build a LangSmith dataset with in-scope questions that have known answers and pages, and out-of-scope questions such as general trivia, with the expected answer 'I don't know'. I run evaluate with an LLM-as-judge evaluator. If the agent refuses valid questions, the trace usually shows a retrieval miss, so I fix chunking or k rather than loosening the prompt. If it answers out-of-scope questions, I strengthen the instruction. The goal is that refusals are tied to missing evidence, not to nervousness.
keyPoints: System prompt restricts answers to retrieved context
Explicit refusal wording
Dataset with both in-scope and out-of-scope questions
Over-refusal often signals a retrieval miss
Measure with evaluate and LLM-as-judge

subjective.question: Compare agentic RAG (retriever as a tool) with a 2-step retrieve-then-generate chain. When would you choose each?
subjective.answer: In a 2-step chain, every request runs one retrieval and then one model call. It is cheap, fast and predictable, and easy to evaluate, because the flow never changes. Its weakness is that it retrieves even for 'hello', and it cannot search again if the first query misses. In agentic RAG, the retriever is a tool given to create_agent. The model decides whether to search, can rewrite the query, and can search several times for multi-part questions. That flexibility costs more tokens and makes latency less predictable. I choose the chain for high-volume, single-hop lookups with strict cost limits, such as a policy FAQ. I choose agentic RAG for a conversational assistant where users mix small talk, follow-ups and multi-part questions that need several searches.
keyPoints: Chain: always exactly one retrieval, cheaper, predictable
Chain cannot skip or repeat retrieval
Agentic: model may skip, rewrite or search several times
Agentic: more flexible but higher and variable cost
Choose based on query complexity and cost constraints

subjective.question: A user says the agent gave a wrong answer. How do you use LangSmith to find the cause?
subjective.answer: Tracing must be on, with LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY set. I open the trace for that run. Each model call and tool call appears, including the query the model sent to the retriever and the chunks returned. First I check the query: did the model search for the right thing? Next I check the retrieved chunks. If none of them contains the correct fact, it is a retrieval miss, and I look at chunking, k, the query wording or the embeddings. If the correct chunk was retrieved but the answer is still wrong, or cites the wrong page, it is a generation error, and I fix the prompt or the model. Finally, I add this question to my evaluation dataset so the fix is tested on every future change.
keyPoints: Enable tracing with LANGSMITH_TRACING and LANGSMITH_API_KEY
Inspect the tool query and returned chunks
Missing evidence means a retrieval miss
Evidence present but answer wrong means a generation error
Add the case to the evaluation dataset

subjective.question: Your prototype uses InMemoryVectorStore. What changes before you ship it, and what do you consider when picking a vector store?
subjective.answer: InMemoryVectorStore lives only in process memory. It is lost on restart and cannot be shared across server replicas, so it is only for notebooks and demos. Before shipping, I move to a persistent vector store, either a self-hosted database or a managed service. I also separate indexing from serving: a separate job loads, splits and embeds the PDFs and writes to the store, and the agent only reads. When choosing a store I consider persistence and backups, metadata filtering so I can restrict by document or department, scale relative to my corpus, latency, hosting cost, data residency rules for Indian clients, and support for updating or deleting documents when a PDF changes. I also store the embedding model name with the index so the query side uses the same model.
keyPoints: InMemoryVectorStore is lost on restart and not shared
Use a persistent store for production
Separate the indexing job from the serving agent
Criteria: filtering, scale, latency, cost, data residency, updates
Record the embedding model with the index

subjective.question: How would you evaluate whether the PDF Q&A agent meets the checkpoint: real page citations and honest refusals?
subjective.answer: I create a LangSmith dataset of examples. Each in-scope example has a question, a reference answer and the correct page. Each out-of-scope example has the reference answer 'I don't know'. My target function calls agent.invoke with the question and returns the final message. I run evaluate(target, data=dataset, evaluators=[...]). For correctness I use openevals create_llm_as_judge with CORRECTNESS_PROMPT, comparing the output to the reference. I add a simple code evaluator that extracts cited page numbers and checks them against the expected page, and another that checks whether out-of-scope answers refuse. Each run is an experiment, so I can compare chunk sizes, k values or prompts side by side and only ship the change that improves the scores without breaking refusals.
keyPoints: Dataset mixes in-scope (answer + page) and out-of-scope examples
evaluate(target, data=dataset, evaluators=[...])
LLM-as-judge with CORRECTNESS_PROMPT
Code evaluators for page accuracy and refusal
Compare experiments before shipping changes

subjective.question: Some PDFs in the folder are scanned images and some have printed page numbers that differ from the PDF page index. How do you handle both?
subjective.answer: PyPDFLoader reads the PDF's text layer. A scanned PDF with no text layer produces empty or near-empty page_content, so those pages are never retrieved, and the agent will wrongly say 'I don't know'. I detect this at indexing time by flagging pages with almost no text. Those files go through OCR before loading, or I use a loader that supports OCR. For numbering, PyPDFLoader's page is the 0-indexed position in the file, but books and reports often have front matter, so printed page 1 may be file page 9. Where page_label is present, I use it for citations, because it matches what the reader sees. Otherwise I show page plus 1 and label it as the PDF page. I log both values in metadata so support staff can trace any citation.
keyPoints: PyPDFLoader relies on the text layer
Scanned pages yield empty content and false refusals
Detect empty pages and apply OCR
Prefer page_label for printed numbering
Otherwise show page + 1 and keep both in metadata

steps.overview: This step moves you from a simple agent loop to explicit control flow with LangGraph. You will model state, wire nodes with normal and conditional edges, add loops, save state with checkpointers, pause for human approval, and combine agents with subagents, subgraphs and Deep Agents. The LangGraph Academy course and agent interviews test exactly these skills: designing the graph, explaining where state lives, and resuming a paused thread.
objectives: Build a StateGraph with a typed state schema and reducers that merge node updates correctly
Wire nodes with add_edge and add_conditional_edges to create branches and bounded retry loops
Persist and resume runs with a checkpointer and a thread_id, and inspect history with get_state_history
Pause a node with interrupt() and resume it with Command(resume=...) for human approval
Choose between subagents-as-tools, subgraphs and create_deep_agent for multi-agent and long-running tasks

concepts.explanation: StateGraph(State) builds a graph whose shared memory is a schema, usually a TypedDict (Pydantic models and dataclasses also work). Every node receives the current state and returns a partial dict of updates, not the whole state. You must call compile() before invoke or stream.

A reducer decides how an update merges into a state key. By default an update overwrites the old value. Annotated[int, operator.add] adds values, and Annotated[list, add_messages] appends messages and replaces by message ID. Use a reducer when parallel nodes write the same key, or they will conflict.
add_node(name, fn) registers a function or runnable as a step. add_edge(START, 'a') sets the entry point and add_edge('a', END) ends the run. A normal edge always goes to the same next node.

add_conditional_edges(source, router_fn, path_options) calls a router that reads state and returns the next node name. A loop is simply a conditional edge that points back to an earlier node. Always add a stop condition, such as an attempts counter, so the loop cannot run forever.

compile(checkpointer=InMemorySaver()) saves a checkpoint of state after every super-step. Checkpoints are grouped by the thread_id passed in config {'configurable': {'thread_id': '...'}}; without it nothing is saved or resumed. Use InMemorySaver for tests and a database saver such as the Postgres checkpointer in production. The Agent Server handles persistence for you.

A checkpointer holds short-term, per-thread state, such as the conversation and graph progress. A store, for example compile(store=InMemoryStore()), holds long-term memory shared across threads, such as user preferences. Exams often ask which one to use for cross-session memory: the answer is the store.

Calling interrupt(payload) inside a node pauses the graph and sends the payload to the caller. A checkpointer is required. You resume with graph.invoke(Command(resume=value), config) on the same thread_id. The node then re-runs from its first line and interrupt() returns value. For create_agent, HumanInTheLoopMiddleware(interrupt_on={...}) gives you approve, edit and reject decisions per tool.

The current pattern is a main create_agent whose tools wrap worker subagents. The main agent acts as supervisor and decides which worker to call. The langgraph-supervisor package is no longer actively maintained, so do not use it in new work. Inside custom graphs, a node can return Command(goto='node', update={...}) to hand off control and update state in one step.

A compiled graph can be added as a node of a parent graph. State keys with the same names are passed between them; if the schemas differ, call the subgraph inside a wrapper node that maps the state. Only the outermost graph gets a checkpointer, and subgraphs inherit persistence from it.

create_deep_agent (from the deepagents package) pre-assembles everything a long-running task needs: a planning to-do tool, a virtual filesystem (ls, read_file, write_file, edit_file), subagents launched through a task tool, summarization and prompt caching. Use it for multi-step research or coding jobs where the context would otherwise overflow.

keyFacts: Nodes return partial updates; the default merge is overwrite unless the key has a reducer in Annotated[...]
add_messages appends new messages and replaces a message that has the same ID; it is the standard reducer for chat history
The checkpointer needs config {'configurable': {'thread_id': ...}} to save or resume; a new thread_id means a fresh state
A checkpoint is written after each super-step; graph.get_state(config) shows the latest one, and graph.get_state_history(config) lists them newest first
interrupt() needs a checkpointer; resume with Command(resume=value) on the same thread_id, and the interrupted node re-runs from its start
With stream_events(..., version='v3'), the recommended way to drive a graph, check stream.interrupted and stream.interrupts to see pauses
Only the outermost graph gets a checkpointer; subgraphs and subagents inherit it
create_agent returns a compiled LangGraph graph, so checkpointers, interrupts and streaming work the same way on it
Loops are bounded by the recursion_limit in config; exceeding it raises GraphRecursionError, so add your own attempts counter as well

example.caption: Corrective RAG graph: a grading router retries retrieval with a rewritten query, at most 3 attempts, with state saved per thread

pitfalls: Forgetting thread_id in config: the checkpointer cannot save or resume, and an interrupted run cannot continue
Writing side effects (API calls, DB writes) before interrupt() in the same node: the node re-runs from the start on resume, so they run twice. Put them after the interrupt or in a separate node
Returning the full state from a node, or appending to a list without a reducer: with the default overwrite, values are silently lost, or parallel writes raise an error
Building a retry loop with no attempts cap: it runs until it hits the recursion limit and raises GraphRecursionError instead of returning a graceful answer
Attaching a checkpointer to subgraphs or subagents, or reaching for langgraph-supervisor: attach it only to the outermost graph, and use the subagents-as-tools pattern
Using the checkpointer for cross-session user memory: a checkpointer is per thread; long-term memory belongs in a store

workflow.title: Rebuild the RAG agent as a graded, resumable graph

steps.label: Define state and reducers
steps.detail: Write a TypedDict with question, docs, attempts (with an operator.add reducer) and answer, or messages with add_messages.

steps.label: Write retrieve, rewrite, generate nodes
steps.detail: Each node reads state and returns only the keys it changes.

steps.label: Add grading conditional edge
steps.detail: A router scores the retrieved docs, using a rule or an LLM grader, and returns 'generate' or 'rewrite'.

steps.label: Close the loop with cap
steps.detail: Send rewrite back to retrieve, and stop retrying once attempts reaches your limit.

steps.label: Compile with a checkpointer
steps.detail: Call compile(checkpointer=InMemorySaver()) and always invoke with a thread_id in config.

steps.label: Add human approval interrupt
steps.detail: Optionally call interrupt() before the final answer is sent, then resume with Command(resume=...) on the same thread.

steps.label: Draw and inspect state
steps.detail: Render the graph with graph.get_graph().draw_mermaid() and walk through get_state_history to show where each checkpoint was saved.

objective.question: A node in your RAG graph returns {'documents': new_docs}. The 'documents' key in the state schema is declared as a plain list[Document] with no Annotated reducer. What happens to the existing documents in state?
options: new_docs is appended to the existing list
LangGraph raises an error because a list key needs a reducer
The update is ignored because nodes must return the full state
They are replaced by new_docs
objective.explanation: Nodes return partial updates, and without a reducer the default merge is overwrite. Appending only happens with a reducer such as operator.add, and nodes never need to return the full state.

objective.question: Your 'messages' key uses Annotated[list, add_messages]. A node returns an AIMessage whose ID matches an AIMessage already in state. What is the result?
options: A duplicate message is appended
All previous messages are cleared and only the new one remains
The new message is dropped silently
The existing message with that ID is replaced
objective.explanation: add_messages appends messages with new IDs and replaces any message that has the same ID. That is why it is the standard reducer for chat history and lets you edit messages.

objective.question: A graph is compiled with a checkpointer. A node calls interrupt({'draft': text}) to ask a human for approval. How do you continue the run with the human's answer?
options: Call graph.update_state() and then invoke with the original input
Re-invoke the graph with the original input; it skips completed nodes automatically
Invoke the graph with Command(resume=answer) and a new thread_id
Invoke the graph with Command(resume=answer) and the same thread_id
objective.explanation: Resuming needs Command(resume=value) on the same thread_id so the checkpointer can load the paused state. A new thread_id starts a fresh state, and re-sending the original input does not resume the pause.

objective.question: A node first inserts a row into a database and then calls interrupt() for approval. After resuming, you find two identical rows. Why, and what is the best fix?
options: The checkpointer replays every node in the graph on resume; switch to a different checkpointer
Command(resume=...) always runs the node twice; resume with update_state instead
The thread_id changed between runs; hard-code the thread_id
The interrupted node re-runs from its start on resume; move the insert after the interrupt or into a separate node
objective.explanation: When resumed, the interrupted node runs again from the beginning, so side effects before interrupt() repeat. Put side effects after the interrupt, in a later node, or make them idempotent.

objective.question: You drive a graph with stream_events(..., version='v3'). How do you detect that the run paused for human input?
options: Catch a GraphInterrupt exception raised to your code
Wait for the stream to end and compare the final state with the input
Poll graph.get_state_history() until a new checkpoint appears
Check stream.interrupted and read the payloads from stream.interrupts
objective.explanation: With stream_events version 'v3', the recommended way to drive a graph, stream.interrupted and stream.interrupts show pauses and their payloads. The other options are indirect or incorrect ways to spot an interrupt.

objective.question: You call graph.get_state_history(config) on a thread that has run several steps. What do you get?
options: A list of checkpoints for all threads, oldest first
Only the latest checkpoint, the same as get_state
The LangSmith traces for the thread
A list of checkpoints for that thread, newest first
objective.explanation: get_state_history lists the checkpoints of the thread in the config, newest first; a checkpoint is written after each super-step. get_state returns only the latest one, and traces live in LangSmith, not the checkpointer.

objective.question: Your support agent must remember a user's preferred language across every new conversation, and each conversation has its own thread_id. Where should this preference live?
options: In the checkpointer, because it already saves state
In a state key with an add_messages reducer
In the recursion_limit config so it persists
In a store passed to compile(store=...), keyed by a user namespace
objective.explanation: The checkpointer saves state per thread, so a new thread_id starts fresh. A store such as InMemoryStore holds long-term memory shared across threads, typically namespaced by user.

objective.question: You build a main agent with create_agent whose tools call two worker subagents, also built with create_agent. You want the whole system to persist and resume. Where should the checkpointer go?
options: On every agent, each with its own InMemorySaver
Nowhere; create_agent persists automatically in local scripts
On each subagent only, so their work is saved separately
Only on the outermost main agent; the subagents inherit it
objective.explanation: Only the outermost graph gets a checkpointer; subgraphs and subagents inherit it. Separate checkpointers fragment state, and automatic persistence is handled by the Agent Server, not by a plain local script.

objective.question: A team wants a supervisor that routes work to a research worker and a writing worker. Following current LangChain guidance, what should they build?
options: One create_agent with every tool from both workers and no structure
Two separate graphs that share a thread_id
A graph using the langgraph-supervisor package
A main create_agent whose tools wrap the worker subagents
objective.explanation: The langgraph-supervisor package is no longer actively maintained; the recommended approach is the subagents pattern, where the main agent calls workers through tools. Merging all tools loses specialisation, and sharing a thread_id across separate graphs is not a coordination pattern.

objective.question: Your corrective RAG graph loops grade_documents -> rewrite_query -> retrieve when results are poor. On a hard question it crashes with GraphRecursionError. What is the best fix?
options: Remove the recursion_limit from config so the loop can run until it succeeds
Replace the conditional edge with a normal edge to generate
Catch GraphRecursionError and restart the graph with a new thread_id
Add an attempts counter to state and route to a fallback answer after a maximum number of retries
objective.explanation: recursion_limit is a safety net; exceeding it raises GraphRecursionError, so you should bound the loop yourself with an attempts counter and a graceful exit. Restarting or removing the grader just hides the problem or removes the retry feature.

objective.question: You add graph.add_conditional_edges('grade_documents', decide_next). What must decide_next do?
options: Return a partial state update that is merged into state
Return True or False only, with True always meaning END
Call the next node function directly
Read the state and return the name of the next node (or a key mapped to it)
objective.explanation: A routing function reads state and returns which node to go to next, optionally via a path map. Nodes return state updates; routers choose edges and do not call nodes themselves.

objective.question: A research task needs many steps: planning, saving notes and large intermediate files, and delegating sub-tasks with clean context. Which option fits best with the least custom code?
options: A single StateGraph node that calls the model once with a long prompt
create_agent with no tools and a larger context window
A Langflow flow exported without any agent components
create_deep_agent, which pre-assembles a filesystem, summarization, subagents and prompt caching
objective.explanation: create_deep_agent is built for long-running tasks and bundles a virtual filesystem, summarization, subagents and prompt caching. The other options either lack planning and delegation or require building it all by hand.

subjective.question: Explain StateGraph, the state schema and reducers. Give an example of when you need a reducer.
subjective.answer: A StateGraph is a graph whose nodes all read and write one shared state. I define the state schema, usually as a TypedDict, listing every key the graph uses, then create StateGraph(State). Each node receives the current state and returns a partial update, only the keys it changes. By default an update overwrites the key. If I want a different merge, I attach a reducer with Annotated. For chat history I use Annotated[list, add_messages], which appends new messages and replaces any message with the same ID. For a list of retrieved documents that should accumulate across retries, I could use Annotated[list, operator.add]. But in a corrective RAG graph I usually want the latest retrieval to replace the old one, so I leave documents as a plain key with overwrite. Choosing the reducer is really choosing how parallel or repeated updates combine.
keyPoints: State schema lists all shared keys, often a TypedDict
Nodes return partial updates
Default merge is overwrite
Reducers via Annotated, e.g. add_messages or operator.add
add_messages appends and replaces by message ID

subjective.question: Draw (describe) your corrective RAG graph from the hands-on task and point to where state is saved.
subjective.answer: My graph goes START -> retrieve -> grade_documents. From grade_documents there is a conditional edge. If enough documents are relevant, it goes to generate and then END. If results are poor and attempts is below the maximum, it goes to rewrite_query, which loops back to retrieve. If attempts reaches the maximum, it goes to a fallback node that answers honestly with what it has, or says it cannot find it. State holds question, documents, attempts, generation and messages. retrieve overwrites documents and increments attempts. I compile with a checkpointer, InMemorySaver for development, and invoke with a thread_id. State is saved as a checkpoint after every super-step, so after retrieve, after grade_documents, after each rewrite and after generate. I can inspect them with get_state_history and see each retry in order, which also helps debugging in LangSmith traces.
keyPoints: retrieve -> grade -> conditional edge to generate, rewrite or fallback
rewrite_query loops back to retrieve
attempts counter bounds the loop
Checkpointer compiled in, thread_id in config
Checkpoint after each super-step, viewable with get_state_history

subjective.question: How do checkpointers and thread_id work together? What happens if you forget the thread_id or change it?
subjective.answer: A checkpointer saves the graph state so a conversation or run can continue later. I pass it at compile time, for example compile(checkpointer=InMemorySaver()), and in production I would use a durable backend; on the Agent Server persistence is handled for me. Every invoke or stream call must include config {'configurable': {'thread_id': '...'}}. The thread_id is the key under which checkpoints are stored. If I call again with the same thread_id, the graph loads the latest checkpoint and continues, so the agent remembers earlier messages. If I use a new thread_id, the state is fresh, like a new conversation. If I forget the thread_id entirely, the checkpointer cannot save or resume, and the call fails. In a web app I usually map one thread_id to one chat session, and keep user-level data in a store instead.
keyPoints: Checkpointer passed to compile()
thread_id in config['configurable'] is required
Same thread_id resumes; new thread_id starts fresh
Missing thread_id means no save or resume
Agent Server handles persistence automatically

subjective.question: What is a super-step, and how do get_state and get_state_history help you debug or time-travel?
subjective.answer: A super-step is one tick of the graph: all nodes scheduled to run at that point execute, possibly in parallel, and their updates are merged through the reducers. After each super-step the checkpointer writes a checkpoint. graph.get_state(config) returns the latest snapshot for the thread, including values and which nodes run next. graph.get_state_history(config) lists all checkpoints for the thread, newest first. For debugging I walk the history to see exactly how state changed, for example how documents and attempts changed on each retrieval retry. For time travel I can pick an earlier checkpoint and resume from its config, or update that state first and then continue, to test a different path without rerunning the whole thread. Combined with LangSmith traces, this tells me both what the model did and what state the graph saved.
keyPoints: Super-step = one round of node execution plus reducer merge
Checkpoint written after each super-step
get_state returns latest snapshot
get_state_history lists checkpoints newest first
Earlier checkpoints enable replay and branching

subjective.question: Explain how you implement human approval with interrupt() in a LangGraph node, and the common pitfalls.
subjective.answer: I call interrupt(payload) inside the node where approval is needed, passing the data the reviewer should see, like a draft email. The graph must have a checkpointer, because the pause is saved as state. The caller sees the pause; with stream_events version 'v3' I check stream.interrupted and read stream.interrupts. After the human decides, I invoke again with Command(resume=value) on the same thread_id. The value becomes the return value of interrupt() inside the node. The main pitfall is that the interrupted node re-runs from its start on resume. So any side effect before interrupt(), like sending a message or writing to a database, runs twice. I keep side effects after the interrupt or in a separate node, or make them idempotent. Other pitfalls are resuming on a different thread_id, which starts fresh, and compiling without a checkpointer.
keyPoints: interrupt(payload) pauses the node
Requires a checkpointer
Resume with Command(resume=value) on the same thread_id
Node re-runs from its start, so avoid side effects before interrupt
Detect pauses via stream.interrupted and stream.interrupts

subjective.question: When would you use HumanInTheLoopMiddleware on create_agent instead of writing interrupt() yourself in a custom StateGraph?
subjective.answer: If my agent is built with create_agent and I just need approval before certain tool calls, HumanInTheLoopMiddleware is the simpler choice. I configure it with interrupt_on, for example {'send_email': {'allowed_decisions': ['approve', 'edit', 'reject']}}, and pass a checkpointer to create_agent. The agent pauses before that tool runs, and the reviewer can approve, edit the arguments or reject. Because create_agent returns a compiled LangGraph graph, resuming works the same way: Command(resume=...) on the same thread_id. I write interrupt() myself when the approval point is not a tool call, for example reviewing a retrieval plan, or when I have a custom StateGraph with its own nodes, like my corrective RAG graph. So middleware covers the common tool-approval case with no graph code, and raw interrupt() gives full control anywhere in a custom graph.
keyPoints: Middleware fits tool-call approval in create_agent
interrupt_on with allowed_decisions approve, edit, reject
Still needs a checkpointer and same thread_id to resume
create_agent returns a compiled graph, so resume mechanics are identical
Raw interrupt() for custom nodes or non-tool approval points

subjective.question: Compare the checkpointer and the store. Give one example of data for each.
subjective.answer: The checkpointer is short-term, thread-scoped memory. It saves the full graph state after each super-step for one thread_id, so a conversation can resume, be inspected or be rewound. Examples are the message history of a chat, the documents retrieved in this run, or a pending interrupt. The store is long-term memory shared across threads. I pass it with compile(store=InMemoryStore()) in development and organise data in namespaces, often by user ID. Nodes can read and write it regardless of which thread is running. Examples are a user's preferred language, facts the agent learned about the user, or saved notes. The simple rule: if the data belongs to one conversation, it is state saved by the checkpointer; if it must survive into new conversations, it goes in the store. Starting a new thread_id gives fresh state but the store data is still there.
keyPoints: Checkpointer: per-thread state, saved each super-step
Store: cross-thread long-term memory
Store organised by namespaces, e.g. user ID
Both passed at compile time
New thread_id resets state but not store

subjective.question: Describe the subagents pattern for multi-agent systems. How does it relate to supervisors and handoffs?
subjective.answer: In the subagents pattern I build one main agent with create_agent. Its tools wrap worker subagents, each its own create_agent with a focused prompt and tool set, such as a researcher and a writer. The main agent acts as the supervisor: it decides which tool to call, the worker runs with clean context, and only its result comes back. This keeps each agent's context small and makes routing an ordinary tool call that I can trace in LangSmith. It is the current recommendation; the langgraph-supervisor package is no longer actively maintained. Handoffs are a different style, where control moves from one agent to another and the receiving agent continues the conversation directly, instead of reporting back to a central one. For persistence, only the outermost graph gets a checkpointer; the subagents inherit it. I prefer subagents when I want central control and clear, testable boundaries.
keyPoints: Main create_agent with tools that wrap worker subagents
Main agent plays supervisor; workers have isolated context
langgraph-supervisor no longer actively maintained
Handoffs transfer control rather than return results
Only outermost graph gets a checkpointer

subjective.question: What is a subgraph in LangGraph, and how do you handle state between a parent graph and a subgraph?
subjective.answer: A subgraph is a compiled graph used as a node, or called from a node, inside a parent graph. I use subgraphs to package reusable pieces, like my retrieve-grade-rewrite loop, or to let a team own one part of a larger system. There are two ways to connect state. If the subgraph shares keys with the parent schema, I can add the compiled subgraph directly as a node, and shared keys flow in and out. If the schemas differ, I write a wrapper node function that maps parent state to the subgraph input, invokes the subgraph, and maps the output back to a parent update. For persistence, I compile only the parent with a checkpointer; the subgraph inherits it, so interrupts inside the subgraph still pause and resume the whole run on the same thread_id. I can also inspect subgraph state when debugging.
keyPoints: Compiled graph used as a node or invoked inside a node
Shared keys: add directly as a node
Different schemas: wrapper function maps state in and out
Only parent gets the checkpointer; subgraph inherits it
Interrupts inside subgraphs resume via the parent thread

subjective.question: What are Deep Agents, and when would you choose create_deep_agent over create_agent?
subjective.answer: Deep Agents are an agent harness for long-running, multi-step tasks. create_deep_agent pre-assembles the pieces such tasks need: planning, a virtual filesystem the agent can write notes and intermediate results to, subagents for delegating focused sub-tasks with clean context, summarization to keep context under control, and prompt caching. Without it I would add these myself as tools and middleware on create_agent. I choose create_deep_agent for open-ended work like deep research, writing a long report or a coding task where the agent must plan, keep large artefacts outside the message history and come back to them later. I choose create_agent for focused agents with a few tools and short loops, like a customer support agent or my RAG agent, where the extra machinery adds cost and complexity. Both are built on LangGraph, so checkpointers, interrupts and streaming work the same way.
keyPoints: Built for long-running, multi-step tasks
Bundles planning, virtual filesystem, subagents, summarization, prompt caching
Filesystem keeps large artefacts out of context
create_agent for simpler, focused agents
Same LangGraph runtime features apply

subjective.question: How do you safely bound a retry loop in LangGraph? Explain recursion_limit and why it is not enough on its own.
subjective.answer: LangGraph lets graphs loop through conditional edges, for example grade_documents sending poor results back to rewrite_query and retrieve. Every graph run has a recursion_limit in config that caps the number of super-steps. If the run exceeds it, LangGraph raises GraphRecursionError. That protects against infinite loops, but it is a crash, not a design. The user gets an error instead of an answer, and the limit counts all steps, not retries of one loop, so it is hard to tune. So I add my own attempts counter to state. The retrieve node increments it, and the routing function checks it: if documents are good, go to generate; if poor and attempts is below my maximum, retry; otherwise go to a fallback node that answers with the best context or says it could not find enough. I keep recursion_limit as a safety net above my own limit.
keyPoints: Loops are built with conditional edges
recursion_limit caps super-steps; exceeding raises GraphRecursionError
Crash is a poor user experience and hard to tune
attempts counter in state checked by the router
Graceful fallback node; keep recursion_limit as safety net

subjective.question: create_agent returns a compiled LangGraph graph. Why does this matter in practice?
subjective.answer: It means everything I learn about LangGraph applies directly to agents built with create_agent. I can pass a checkpointer and run it with a thread_id, so the agent remembers a conversation and can resume. I can inspect it with get_state and get_state_history. Interrupts work the same way, whether they come from HumanInTheLoopMiddleware or a node, and I resume with Command(resume=...) on the same thread_id. I can stream it with stream_events version 'v3' and watch for stream.interrupted. I can use it as a subagent behind a tool, or as a node or subgraph inside a bigger StateGraph, remembering that only the outermost graph gets the checkpointer. It also works with LangSmith tracing and LangSmith Studio through langgraph dev, and can be deployed on the Agent Server. So I start with create_agent and only drop to a custom StateGraph when I need explicit control flow like my grading loop.
keyPoints: Same checkpointer and thread_id behaviour
Same interrupt and Command(resume) mechanics
Same streaming with stream_events v3
Composable as subagent or subgraph; outermost graph holds checkpointer
Works with LangSmith, Studio and Agent Server

steps.overview: This step teaches you to make agent behaviour visible and measurable with LangSmith. You will turn on tracing, read traces to debug prompts, tool calls, latency and tokens, then build datasets and run experiments that score prompt changes. The LangSmith course and real agent work both expect you to prove an improvement with numbers, not by feel.
objectives: Enable LangSmith tracing for any LangChain or LangGraph app using LANGSMITH_TRACING and LANGSMITH_API_KEY.
Read a trace tree to find the exact prompt, tool call, latency and token cost of each step.
Create a dataset of examples and write code and LLM-as-judge evaluators.
Run and compare experiments with evaluate() to show a score change caused by a prompt edit.
Version prompts and debug a local agent in LangSmith Studio with langgraph dev and langgraph.json.

concepts.explanation: Setting LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY makes LangChain and LangGraph send every run to LangSmith automatically, with no code change. LANGSMITH_PROJECT picks the project the traces land in. For plain Python functions or non-LangChain SDK calls, add the @traceable decorator from langsmith.

A trace is one end-to-end request, shown as a tree of runs. Each run has a type such as chain, llm, tool or retriever, plus inputs, outputs, start and end time, and errors. For a create_agent graph you see the model node, each tool call and its arguments, and the loop back to the model.

Each LLM run records latency and token usage (prompt and completion tokens) and, where the model is priced, estimated cost. The trace view rolls these up to the parent, so you can spot the slow step or the call that blew up the context. Use this to justify middleware like SummarizationMiddleware or a cheaper model.

A dataset is a named collection of examples. Each example has inputs (what the target receives) and optional reference outputs (the expected answer). You can create examples in code with Client.create_examples, upload a CSV, or add runs from production traces to a dataset.

An evaluator is a function that scores one run. In the Python SDK it can take inputs, outputs and reference_outputs and return a bool, a number or a dict with a key and score. Use code evaluators for exact checks (format, keyword, tool used) and LLM-as-judge for open-ended quality.

openevals provides create_llm_as_judge(prompt=CORRECTNESS_PROMPT, model=..., feedback_key=...) which returns an evaluator that asks a judge model to grade the output against the reference. Prebuilt prompts like CORRECTNESS_PROMPT save time, but you should spot-check judge scores against your own judgement.

evaluate(target, data=dataset, evaluators=[...]) runs the target on every example, applies every evaluator and saves the results as one experiment. Use experiment_prefix to name it, for example prompt-v1. Two experiments on the same dataset can be opened side by side in the comparison view to see per-example wins, losses and aggregate scores.

LangSmith stores prompts with a commit history; you push new versions and pull a specific version or tag in code, so experiments map to exact prompt versions. LangSmith Studio connects to your agent running locally via the LangGraph CLI (langgraph dev) using a langgraph.json config. In Studio you can run the graph, inspect state at each node, step through interrupts and edit inputs.

keyFacts: Minimum tracing setup: LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY=<key>; add LANGSMITH_PROJECT to choose a project, otherwise traces go to the default project.
LangChain and LangGraph code is traced automatically once the env vars are set; use @traceable for your own functions.
An example = inputs + optional reference outputs; a dataset is a set of examples; an experiment = one run of a target over a dataset with evaluators.
evaluate(target, data=..., evaluators=[...], experiment_prefix=...) is the core API; the target takes the example inputs dict and returns an outputs dict.
Evaluator arguments by name: inputs, outputs, reference_outputs; return a bool, a number, or a dict with key and score.
openevals: create_llm_as_judge(prompt=CORRECTNESS_PROMPT, model=..., feedback_key="correctness") for an LLM-as-judge evaluator.
Decision rule: compare two prompts on the same dataset, with the same evaluators and the same model; change only one thing per experiment.
LangSmith Studio needs langgraph.json (dependencies, graphs, env) and the local server started with langgraph dev.
Use the comparison view to read per-example regressions, not just the average score.

example.caption: Build a 20-example dataset and compare two system prompts with an LLM-as-judge correctness evaluator.
example.code:
# env: LANGSMITH_TRACING=true, LANGSMITH_API_KEY=..., plus model provider keys
from langsmith import Client, evaluate
from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model
from openevals.llm import create_llm_as_judge
from openevals.prompts import CORRECTNESS_PROMPT

PAIRS = [("How do I reset my password?", "Use Settings > Security > Reset.")]  # extend to 20 pairs
V1 = "You are a support bot."
V2 = "You are a support bot. Answer in 2 sentences using only product facts. Say 'I don't know' if unsure."

client = Client()
ds = client.create_dataset("support-faq-20")
client.create_examples(dataset_id=ds.id, examples=[
    {"inputs": {"question": q}, "outputs": {"answer": a}} for q, a in PAIRS])

model = init_chat_model("anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5", temperature=0)

def make_target(system_prompt):
    def target(inputs: dict) -> dict:
        msg = model.invoke([{"role": "system", "content": system_prompt},
                            {"role": "user", "content": inputs["question"]}])
        return {"answer": msg.content}
    return target

judge = create_llm_as_judge(prompt=CORRECTNESS_PROMPT, model="openai:o3-mini", feedback_key="correctness")
def correctness(inputs, outputs, reference_outputs):
    return judge(inputs=inputs, outputs=outputs, reference_outputs=reference_outputs)

for name, sp in [("prompt-v1", V1), ("prompt-v2", V2)]:
    evaluate(make_target(sp), data="support-faq-20", evaluators=[correctness],
             experiment_prefix=name, max_concurrency=4)

pitfalls: Setting only the API key and forgetting LANGSMITH_TRACING=true, so nothing appears in the UI.
Changing the prompt and the model (or temperature) in the same experiment, so you cannot say which change moved the score.
Trusting an LLM judge blindly; always read a few low and high scored examples to confirm the judge agrees with you.
A target that returns a string instead of a dict, or uses keys that the evaluator does not read, breaking scoring.
Quoting the average only; a better mean can hide new failures on specific examples that the comparison view would show.
Putting secrets in langgraph.json; reference an .env file through the env field instead.

workflow.title: From tracing to a proven prompt improvement

steps.label: Enable tracing
steps.detail: Set LANGSMITH_TRACING=true, LANGSMITH_API_KEY and LANGSMITH_PROJECT, then run the agent once.

steps.label: Read the trace
steps.detail: Open the trace tree and check the prompt, tool calls, latency and tokens to find the weak step.

steps.label: Build the dataset
steps.detail: Create 20 examples with inputs and reference outputs, mixing easy, hard and edge cases.

steps.label: Write evaluators
steps.detail: Add a code check plus an openevals LLM-as-judge correctness evaluator.

steps.label: Run baseline experiment
steps.detail: Call evaluate() with the current prompt under an experiment_prefix like prompt-v1.
